newsitem.title: USA: Wheat damage likely from pending frigid cold-trade.
newsitem.headline: Wheat damage likely from pending frigid cold-trade.

text.p: A snowstorm that hit northern Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas Friday, will be replaced this weekend by frigid cold which crop sources said poses a serious threat to wheat in Kansas and Oklahoma.
"There is potential it could be very serious (threat) to the wheat, particularly in Oklahoma and southern Kansas," said Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp.
Temperatures were forecast in the upper teens Fahrenheit early Saturday in southwest Kansas to the northern Texas Panhandle and 28 degrees or less throughout the rest of Oklahoma, Burgio said.
Much of the wheat in those states is at the jointing stage, in which the seed-producing head of the plant starts moving up stalks called tillers. A severe freeze now would kill the tillers.
"What likely will happen is the tillers jointing now will be killed," said Gary Paulsen, an agronomy professor at Kansas State University.
The freeze-damaged wheat plants should produce replacement tillers, but these often are lower yielding, he said.

As of last Sunday, 83 percent of Oklahoma's wheat and 45 percent of Kansas wheat was jointing, according to the state's agricultural statistics services. Jointing progress was not available for Texas wheat from its agricultural statistics service office.
However, the two to six inches of snow expected Friday in Kansas could insulate some fields from the cold, thus minimizing damage, said WSC's Burgio.
Soft red winter wheat in northeast Arkansas and in southeast Missouri may be in jeopardy as well. Freezing weather was forecast to move into those areas Monday, said Burgio.
